overview: Databricks Asset Bundles (DABs) are the native infrastructure-as-code (IaC) framework for packaging, versioning, and deploying Databricks projects, jobs, DLT pipelines, notebooks, and ML resources as a single declarative unit described in a databricks.yml file.

A bundle bundles together source artifacts (notebooks, Python wheels, SQL) and resource definitions (jobs, pipelines, schemas, experiments) plus per-environment targets (dev/staging/prod), enabling reproducible, promotable deployments through the Databricks CLI.

DABs, combined with a CI/CD system such as GitHub Actions, replace ad hoc notebook copying, the legacy dbx tool, and Terraform-only setups, giving teams a Git-driven, reviewable, and auditable deployment lifecycle for the whole Databricks project.
learningObjectives: Understand the structure of a databricks.yml bundle configuration: the bundle, include, resources, targets, and variables mappings and how they compose.
Deploy the same code to dev, staging, and prod using targets, mode: development vs production, per-target overrides, and variable substitution like ${var.x} and ${bundle.target}.
Wire a full CI/CD pipeline with GitHub Actions that runs databricks bundle validate on pull requests and databricks bundle deploy on merge, authenticating via OAuth service principals or OIDC.
Master the core Databricks CLI (Go-based v0.2xx+) bundle commands: validate, deploy, run, and destroy, and know when each runs in the lifecycle.
coreConcept.formalDefinition: A Databricks Asset Bundle is a declarative, YAML-defined project artifact (rooted at a databricks.yml file) that specifies a bundle's identity, the source files to sync, the Databricks resources to create (jobs, DLT pipelines, schemas, ML experiments, model serving endpoints, etc.), and one or more named targets (deployment environments) with mode and workspace configuration. The Databricks CLI reads this configuration, resolves variables and target overrides, builds any artifacts (e.g., Python wheels), uploads files to the workspace, and creates or updates the corresponding resources through the Databricks REST APIs (internally using a Terraform provider), producing a reproducible deployment that can be validated, deployed, run, and destroyed from the command line and from CI/CD.
coreConcept.simpleExplanation: Think of a Databricks Asset Bundle as a shipping container for your entire Databricks project. Instead of manually copying notebooks and clicking around the UI to create jobs, you write one YAML file that says 'here is my code, here are my jobs and pipelines, and here is how they should look in dev versus prod.' Then a single command (databricks bundle deploy) ships that whole container to the right environment, and your CI/CD system does it automatically whenever code is merged.
coreConcept.historicalContext: Before DABs, Databricks teams stitched together deployment with notebook Git sync, the Jobs REST API, and community/experimental tools. The most popular was dbx (Databricks eXtensions), which packaged jobs and enabled CI/CD but was a separate Python tool with its own conventions. Many enterprises used the Databricks Terraform provider for full IaC, which was powerful but heavyweight for application-level jobs. In 2023 Databricks introduced Asset Bundles (initially in Public Preview, GA in 2024) as a first-class, CLI-native successor. They ship in the new Go-based Databricks CLI (v0.200+), officially deprecating dbx and providing a lighter, opinionated IaC path that still uses Terraform under the hood but hides that complexity for typical job/pipeline deployment.

whyItMatters.business: Bundles turn Databricks deployments into a repeatable, auditable software-delivery process, reducing time-to-production for data products, shrinking release risk, and giving auditors a Git history of exactly what was deployed to prod and by whom.
whyItMatters.engineering: Engineers get one source of truth for code plus infrastructure, code review on every change via PRs, environment parity between dev and prod, and the ability to spin up isolated per-developer deployments without collision.
whyItMatters.scalability: As the number of jobs, pipelines, and teams grows, declarative bundles with variables and targets scale far better than hand-maintained UI configuration or copy-pasted JSON, and can be templated across dozens of projects.
whyItMatters.cost: Dev-mode deployments pause schedules and prefix resources so they do not run expensive production workloads accidentally; managing compute as code lets teams standardize right-sized clusters and avoid orphaned, always-on all-purpose clusters.
whyItMatters.reliability: CI/CD gates (validate on PR, automated tests, deploy on merge) catch configuration errors before they reach prod, and idempotent bundle deploys ensure the deployed state always matches the reviewed YAML, eliminating configuration drift.

coreComponents.name: databricks.yml (Bundle Configuration File)
coreComponents.definition: The root YAML file that defines the bundle. It contains the top-level bundle mapping (name, optional git and uuid), and typically include, variables, resources, and targets mappings.
coreComponents.purpose: To declaratively describe the entire project: its identity, which files compose it, what Databricks resources it creates, and how those differ per environment.
coreComponents.responsibilities: Names the bundle, references included resource files, declares variables and their defaults, and defines targets that override configuration for dev/staging/prod.
coreComponents.examples: A databricks.yml at the repo root with `bundle: { name: sales_etl }`, an include list pulling in resources/*.yml, and targets for dev and prod.

coreComponents.name: Resources (Jobs, Pipelines, Schemas, Experiments)
coreComponents.definition: The resources mapping declares the Databricks objects the bundle manages: jobs, DLT pipelines, Unity Catalog schemas, MLflow experiments, model serving endpoints, clusters, quality monitors, and more.
coreComponents.purpose: To express infrastructure-as-code for the actual runtime assets so they are created and updated consistently on every deploy.
coreComponents.responsibilities: Defines each resource's configuration (tasks, clusters, triggers, libraries, permissions) which the CLI translates into REST API/Terraform calls.
coreComponents.examples: resources.jobs.daily_etl with two tasks; resources.pipelines.bronze_dlt with a target schema; resources.schemas.analytics in a catalog.

coreComponents.name: Targets (Deployment Environments)
coreComponents.definition: Named environments (e.g., dev, staging, prod) under the targets mapping, each specifying a workspace host, a mode (development or production), a default flag, and per-target overrides of variables and resources.
coreComponents.purpose: To promote the same code across environments with environment-specific behavior (different workspaces, cluster sizes, schedules, run-as identities).
coreComponents.responsibilities: Sets the deployment root path, run-as identity, mode-driven behavior (prefixing, schedule pausing), and merges overrides on top of base resource definitions.
coreComponents.examples: targets.dev with mode: development and default: true; targets.prod with mode: production, a service-principal run_as, and a fixed schedule.

coreComponents.name: Variables and Substitution
coreComponents.definition: User-declared variables (under variables) and built-in substitution references (like ${bundle.target}, ${workspace.current_user.userName}, ${var.catalog}) that parameterize the configuration.
coreComponents.purpose: To keep configuration DRY and environment-agnostic by injecting values that change per target or per developer.
coreComponents.responsibilities: Provide defaults, accept overrides per target or via CLI/env, and resolve at deploy time into concrete values.
coreComponents.examples: var.warehouse_id referenced as ${var.warehouse_id}; a table name built as ${var.catalog}.${bundle.target}.orders.

coreComponents.name: Databricks CLI (Bundle Commands)
coreComponents.definition: The Go-based Databricks CLI (v0.200+) provides the bundle subcommands validate, deploy, run, destroy, summary, and generate that operate on the databricks.yml.
coreComponents.purpose: To execute the bundle lifecycle from a terminal or CI/CD runner in a scriptable, authenticated way.
coreComponents.responsibilities: Parses and validates config, resolves variables/targets, builds artifacts, syncs files, applies resource changes via the internal Terraform state, and triggers runs.
coreComponents.examples: `databricks bundle validate -t prod`, `databricks bundle deploy -t prod`, `databricks bundle run daily_etl -t prod`.

internalWorking: When you run a bundle command, the CLI loads databricks.yml, merges any files listed under include, and applies the selected target's overrides on top of the base configuration to produce a single resolved configuration tree.

Variable and substitution references (${var.x}, ${bundle.target}, ${workspace.current_user.userName}) are resolved against declared variables, CLI/env overrides, target values, and workspace context; validate fails fast if any required value is missing.

For deploy, the CLI builds declared artifacts (e.g., compiles a Python wheel via the artifacts mapping), then syncs source files to a deployment root path in the workspace (in dev mode, under /Users/<you>/.bundle/<name>/<target>).

The CLI translates the resolved resources into a Terraform configuration internally and applies it, storing Terraform state in the workspace so subsequent deploys are idempotent and only push the diff; destroy tears the resources down using that same state.

In development mode the CLI transparently prefixes resource names with [dev <username>], pauses job/pipeline schedules, and tags resources so concurrent developers do not collide; production mode deploys clean, unprefixed resources with schedules active.
coreConcept.architectureFlow: Developer writes code + databricks.yml -> git push / open PR -> CI runs databricks bundle validate -t staging -> merge to main -> CI runs databricks bundle deploy -t prod (authenticated via OAuth SP / OIDC) -> CLI resolves targets/variables + builds wheel -> syncs files to workspace + applies Terraform-backed resources -> Jobs/DLT pipelines created/updated -> databricks bundle run triggers execution -> monitoring/alerts
dataFlowWalkthrough: 1. A developer edits notebooks/Python and the databricks.yml, then runs `databricks bundle validate -t dev` locally to catch schema and reference errors.
2. They run `databricks bundle deploy -t dev`, which deploys an isolated, schedule-paused, name-prefixed copy of the jobs into their own workspace path for testing.
3. They open a pull request; GitHub Actions checks out the code, installs the Databricks CLI, and runs `databricks bundle validate -t staging` as a required PR check.
4. On merge to main, a second workflow authenticates via an OAuth service principal (or OIDC) and runs `databricks bundle deploy -t prod`.

5. The CLI builds the wheel, uploads artifacts, and applies the prod resources; a follow-up `databricks bundle run` (or the scheduled trigger) executes the pipeline, with run status and alerts surfaced back to the team.

keyTerminology.meaning: A project defined by a databricks.yml that packages source files and resource definitions together with deployment targets.
keyTerminology.importance: It is the unit of deployment and versioning; everything in DABs is organized around the bundle.

keyTerminology.meaning: A named deployment environment (dev, staging, prod) with its own workspace host, mode, and configuration overrides.
keyTerminology.importance: Targets are how the same code is promoted across environments with environment-specific behavior.

keyTerminology.meaning: A per-target setting: development prefixes and pauses resources for isolated dev; production deploys clean, schedule-active resources with strict validation.
keyTerminology.importance: Mode drives safety behavior, preventing accidental prod runs and enabling per-developer isolation.

keyTerminology.meaning: References like ${var.x}, ${bundle.target}, and ${workspace.current_user.userName} that resolve to concrete values at deploy time.
keyTerminology.importance: Enables DRY, environment-agnostic configuration and per-developer/per-target parameterization.

keyTerminology.meaning: The rewritten command-line tool that natively supports bundle validate/deploy/run/destroy and OAuth authentication.
keyTerminology.importance: It is the execution engine for bundles both locally and in CI/CD; the legacy Python CLI does not support bundles.

importantConcepts.concept: Terraform Under the Hood, Hidden by the CLI
importantConcepts.explanation: DABs internally generate and apply a Terraform configuration and store Terraform state in the workspace, giving idempotent, diff-based deploys and a destroy path. Engineers get IaC benefits without authoring HCL, though understanding this explains behaviors like state locking and drift correction.

Setting mode: development makes the CLI prefix all resource names with [dev <username>], pause schedules and triggers, and tag resources, so multiple developers can deploy the same bundle into a shared workspace without clobbering each other or firing scheduled prod-like runs.

variationsAndTypes: **Job/Pipeline Bundles:** The most common form, deploying Workflows jobs and DLT pipelines as code.
**ML/MLOps Bundles:** Deploy MLflow experiments, registered models, model serving endpoints, and training jobs for reproducible model promotion.
**Bundle Templates:** Reusable scaffolds (default-python, dbt, ML, or custom templates via `databricks bundle init`) that standardize project structure across an organization.
**Monorepo vs Multi-repo Bundles:** A single bundle per repo, or multiple bundles composed via include across a larger monorepo of data products.
advantages: **Single Source of Truth:** Code and infrastructure (jobs, pipelines, schemas) live together in Git, versioned and reviewable.
**Environment Parity and Promotion:** The same config deploys to dev/staging/prod via targets, eliminating snowflake environments.
**Idempotent, Drift-Free Deploys:** Terraform-backed state means deploys converge the environment to the declared config.
**Native CI/CD Integration:** First-class CLI commands (validate/deploy/run) drop cleanly into GitHub Actions, Azure DevOps, or GitLab.
**Developer Isolation via Dev Mode:** Prefixing and schedule pausing let many engineers work safely in a shared workspace.
disadvantages: **YAML Complexity:** Large bundles with many overrides and substitutions can become hard to read and debug.
**Learning Curve vs UI:** Teams used to clicking through the Jobs UI must learn declarative config and CLI workflows.
**Terraform State Sensitivity:** Because state lives in the workspace, manual UI edits to bundle-managed resources cause drift that deploys will overwrite.
**Less Flexible Than Raw Terraform:** For account-level or complex networking infrastructure, the Databricks Terraform provider is still more expressive than bundles.

tradeOffs.whenToUse: Use Asset Bundles for application-level deployment of jobs, DLT pipelines, and ML assets that should follow a Git-based, environment-promoted CI/CD lifecycle, especially when replacing dbx or manual UI/JSON deployment.
tradeOffs.whenToAvoid: Avoid relying on bundles alone for account/workspace provisioning, complex multi-cloud networking, or organization-wide governance infrastructure, where the full Databricks Terraform provider or a dedicated platform IaC layer is more appropriate.

coreConcept.realWorldAnalogy: A Databricks Asset Bundle is like a Docker image plus a docker-compose file for your Databricks project: the image packages your application (notebooks, wheels), and the compose/manifest declares the services (jobs, pipelines) and how they run in different environments. `databricks bundle deploy -t prod` is the equivalent of `docker compose up` against your production stack, and CI/CD automates it on every merge.

commonMisconceptions.myth: Asset Bundles are just a fancy way to upload notebooks.
commonMisconceptions.reality: Bundles deploy full infrastructure-as-code: jobs, DLT pipelines, schemas, experiments, permissions, and clusters, not just source files. They manage the lifecycle of these resources with idempotent, state-backed deploys.

commonMisconceptions.myth: I still need dbx or the old Python CLI for CI/CD.
commonMisconceptions.reality: dbx is deprecated in favor of DABs, and bundle commands require the new Go-based CLI (v0.200+). Modern CI/CD uses databricks bundle validate/deploy/run exclusively.

productionConsiderations.scalability: Bundles scale across many jobs and teams by splitting configuration into included files, parameterizing with variables, and templating projects with `bundle init`; a single CI/CD pipeline can deploy dozens of resources idempotently.
productionConsiderations.reliability: validate-on-PR and deploy-on-merge gates plus idempotent, state-backed deploys keep the deployed state aligned with the reviewed config, reducing drift-related incidents.
productionConsiderations.faultTolerance: If a deploy fails partway, Terraform state records what succeeded so a re-run converges safely; jobs should still define retries and idempotent writes for runtime resilience.
productionConsiderations.monitoring: Deployed jobs and pipelines surface run status via Workflows, system tables, and the Jobs API; CI/CD logs record every validate/deploy with the exact commit and target.
productionConsiderations.security: Authenticate CI/CD with OAuth service principals or OIDC (never long-lived personal tokens), store secrets in environment secrets, set run_as to a dedicated service principal in prod, and manage resource permissions in the bundle.
productionConsiderations.costOptimization: Use dev mode to pause schedules and prevent accidental prod-scale runs, define right-sized job clusters as code, and destroy ephemeral per-developer deployments to reclaim resources.
productionConsiderations.performance: Keep bundles focused, use include to modularize, cache the CLI in CI runners, and prefer job (ephemeral) clusters defined in the bundle to minimize both deploy time and runtime cost.

codeExamples.title: A Complete databricks.yml with Bundle, Variables, Resources, and Targets
codeExamples.overview: This is a canonical databricks.yml defining a bundle, declaring variables, including a resource file, and configuring dev and prod targets with mode-driven behavior and per-target overrides.
codeExamples.code:
bundle:
  name: sales_etl

include:
  - resources/*.yml

variables:
  catalog:
    description: Unity Catalog to write into
    default: main
  warehouse_id:
    description: SQL warehouse id for dashboards
    default: ""
  notifications_email:
    default: data-eng@example.com

resources:
  jobs:
    daily_sales_etl:
      name: daily_sales_etl
      tasks:
        - task_key: ingest_bronze
          notebook_task:
            notebook_path: ../src/bronze_ingest.py
          job_cluster_key: etl_cluster
        - task_key: build_silver
          depends_on:
            - task_key: ingest_bronze
          notebook_task:
            notebook_path: ../src/silver_build.py
          job_cluster_key: etl_cluster
      job_clusters:
        - job_cluster_key: etl_cluster
          new_cluster:
            spark_version: 15.4.x-scala2.12
            node_type_id: i3.xlarge
            num_workers: 2
      email_notifications:
        on_failure:
          - ${var.notifications_email}

targets:
  dev:
    mode: development
    default: true
    workspace:
      host: https://dbc-dev.cloud.databricks.com
    variables:
      catalog: dev

  prod:
    mode: production
    workspace:
      host: https://dbc-prod.cloud.databricks.com
      root_path: /Workspace/Shared/.bundle/${bundle.name}/${bundle.target}
    variables:
      catalog: main
    run_as:
      service_principal_name: 7a9f...-sp-etl
    resources:
      jobs:
        daily_sales_etl:
          schedule:
            quartz_cron_expression: "0 0 3 * * ?"
            timezone_id: UTC
codeExamples.breakdown: bundle.name identifies the project. include pulls in extra resource YAML. variables declares catalog, warehouse_id, and an email with defaults. resources.jobs defines a two-task job with a shared job cluster and a failure email referencing ${var.notifications_email}. targets.dev is the default with mode: development (auto prefix/pause), and targets.prod uses mode: production, a service-principal run_as, a fixed root_path, and overrides catalog to main while adding a production schedule.
codeExamples.expectedOutput: `databricks bundle validate -t prod` returns 'Validation OK!'; `databricks bundle deploy -t prod` creates the daily_sales_etl job (unprefixed, scheduled at 03:00 UTC, running as the service principal) in the prod workspace.
codeExamples.commonIssues: Relative notebook_path resolved from the wrong directory; forgetting default: true on a dev target so no target is selected; leaving warehouse_id empty when a resource requires it; YAML indentation errors under the nested override maps.
codeExamples.optimizationTips: Keep resources in separate files under resources/ and pull them in via include; use variables for anything that differs per environment; prefer job clusters over all-purpose clusters; set run_as to a service principal in prod for consistent identity.

codeExamples.title: Databricks CLI Bundle Lifecycle Commands
codeExamples.overview: The core commands for the bundle lifecycle using the Go-based Databricks CLI (v0.200+), from validation through deploy, run, and teardown, including authentication via environment variables.
codeExamples.code:
# Install / verify the new Go-based CLI (v0.2xx+)
databricks --version

# Authenticate (option A: host + PAT via env vars)
export DATABRICKS_HOST=https://dbc-prod.cloud.databricks.com
export DATABRICKS_TOKEN=dapiXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX

# Authenticate (option B: OAuth machine-to-machine service principal)
export DATABRICKS_HOST=https://dbc-prod.cloud.databricks.com
export DATABRICKS_CLIENT_ID=<sp-application-id>
export DATABRICKS_CLIENT_SECRET=<sp-oauth-secret>

# 1. Validate the resolved configuration for a target
databricks bundle validate -t prod

# 2. Deploy the bundle (build wheel, sync files, apply resources)
databricks bundle deploy -t prod

# 3. Trigger a job/pipeline defined in the bundle and wait for completion
databricks bundle run daily_sales_etl -t prod

# Inspect what was deployed
databricks bundle summary -t prod

# 4. Tear everything down (e.g., an ephemeral dev deployment)
databricks bundle destroy -t dev --auto-approve
codeExamples.breakdown: validate resolves targets/variables and checks the config without touching the workspace. deploy builds artifacts, syncs source files, and applies the Terraform-backed resources idempotently. run triggers a named resource (job or pipeline) and streams status. summary prints deployed resource URLs. destroy removes bundle-managed resources using stored state; --auto-approve skips the confirmation prompt for CI.
codeExamples.expectedOutput: validate prints 'Validation OK!'; deploy prints uploaded file paths and 'Deployment complete!'; run prints the run URL and final state (e.g., SUCCESS); destroy prints the resources removed.
codeExamples.commonIssues: Using the old Python CLI which lacks bundle subcommands; missing/expired DATABRICKS_TOKEN or wrong OAuth credentials; selecting a target that does not exist; state lock errors if two deploys run concurrently against the same target.
codeExamples.optimizationTips: Pin the CLI version in CI for reproducibility; prefer OAuth service-principal credentials over PATs; use -t explicitly in automation rather than relying on the default target; run validate as a fast pre-check before deploy.

codeExamples.title: GitHub Actions Workflow: Validate on PR, Deploy on Merge (OIDC)
codeExamples.overview: A CI/CD pipeline that runs databricks bundle validate on pull requests to staging and databricks bundle deploy to prod on merges to main, authenticating with OAuth service principals stored as environment secrets.
codeExamples.code:
name: databricks-cicd

on:
  pull_request:
    branches: [ main ]
  push:
    branches: [ main ]

jobs:
  validate:
    if: github.event_name == 'pull_request'
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    environment: staging
    env:
      DATABRICKS_HOST: ${{ vars.DATABRICKS_HOST_STAGING }}
      DATABRICKS_CLIENT_ID: ${{ secrets.DATABRICKS_CLIENT_ID }}
      DATABRICKS_CLIENT_SECRET: ${{ secrets.DATABRICKS_CLIENT_SECRET }}
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: databricks/setup-cli@main
      - name: Validate bundle
        run: databricks bundle validate -t staging

  deploy:
    if: github.event_name == 'push'
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    environment: prod
    env:
      DATABRICKS_HOST: ${{ vars.DATABRICKS_HOST_PROD }}
      DATABRICKS_CLIENT_ID: ${{ secrets.DATABRICKS_CLIENT_ID }}
      DATABRICKS_CLIENT_SECRET: ${{ secrets.DATABRICKS_CLIENT_SECRET }}
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: databricks/setup-cli@main
      - name: Deploy to prod
        run: databricks bundle deploy -t prod
      - name: Smoke-run pipeline
        run: databricks bundle run daily_sales_etl -t prod
codeExamples.breakdown: The workflow triggers on pull_request and push to main. The validate job runs only on PRs, using the staging service principal to run bundle validate as a required check. The deploy job runs only on merges to main, uses GitHub Environments (prod) for protection/approvals, authenticates with the prod service principal via env secrets, deploys the bundle, and smoke-runs the job. databricks/setup-cli installs the Go-based CLI on the runner.
codeExamples.expectedOutput: On a PR, the validate check passes green if the config is valid. On merge, deploy uploads artifacts and applies resources, then the smoke run reports SUCCESS; failures fail the workflow and block/alert.
codeExamples.commonIssues: Storing credentials as repo-wide secrets instead of per-environment; not gating the prod environment with required reviewers; using a PAT that expires; forgetting to set DATABRICKS_HOST as an environment variable; CLI version mismatch across runs.
codeExamples.optimizationTips: Use GitHub Environments with required reviewers for prod; scope one service principal per environment with least privilege; prefer OIDC federation to eliminate stored secrets entirely; cache the CLI and pin its version for reproducible runs.

codeExamples.title: Building and Deploying a Python Wheel as a Bundle Artifact
codeExamples.overview: Bundles can build a Python wheel from the project and attach it as a job library, so shared library code is packaged and versioned alongside the deployment.
codeExamples.code:
bundle:
  name: ml_scoring

artifacts:
  scoring_lib:
    type: whl
    build: python -m build --wheel
    path: ./libs/scoring

resources:
  jobs:
    batch_scoring:
      name: batch_scoring
      tasks:
        - task_key: score
          python_wheel_task:
            package_name: scoring
            entry_point: run_scoring
          libraries:
            - whl: ${artifacts.scoring_lib.path}/dist/*.whl
          job_cluster_key: score_cluster
      job_clusters:
        - job_cluster_key: score_cluster
          new_cluster:
            spark_version: 15.4.x-scala2.12
            node_type_id: i3.xlarge
            num_workers: 4

targets:
  dev:
    mode: development
    default: true
  prod:
    mode: production
codeExamples.breakdown: The artifacts.scoring_lib mapping tells the CLI to build a wheel by running the build command in the given path during deploy. The python_wheel_task references the built package by name and entry point, and the libraries entry attaches the freshly built wheel via the ${artifacts...} substitution. On deploy, the CLI builds the wheel, uploads it, and wires it to the job.
codeExamples.expectedOutput: `databricks bundle deploy -t prod` compiles the wheel (visible in ./libs/scoring/dist/), uploads it to the workspace, and creates a batch_scoring job whose task installs that wheel and runs the run_scoring entry point.
codeExamples.commonIssues: Missing build backend (need `pip install build`); package_name/entry_point not matching setup.cfg/pyproject.toml; wheel glob not matching if the version changes; Python version mismatch between build host and cluster runtime.
codeExamples.optimizationTips: Define entry points in pyproject.toml so python_wheel_task stays stable across versions; keep library code out of notebooks for testability; pin the runtime spark_version so the wheel's dependencies resolve consistently.

endToEndExample.businessProblem: A retail analytics team maintains a nightly sales ETL job and a DLT pipeline that were previously deployed by manually cloning notebooks and clicking through the Jobs UI, causing drift between environments, no code review, and occasional accidental prod runs from dev testing. They need a Git-driven, reviewable, environment-promoted deployment process.
endToEndExample.inputData: A repo containing PySpark notebooks (bronze_ingest.py, silver_build.py), a shared Python wheel of transformation utilities, and a databricks.yml describing a job and a DLT pipeline; raw sales files land in cloud storage read by the pipeline.
endToEndExample.architecture: A single Asset Bundle at the repo root with resources split under resources/, variables for catalog and warehouse, and targets for dev (mode: development, default), staging, and prod (mode: production, service-principal run_as). GitHub Actions runs validate on PRs and deploy on merges to main, authenticating each environment with its own OAuth service principal via GitHub Environment secrets.
processingSteps: 1. A developer branches, edits notebooks and databricks.yml, then runs `databricks bundle validate -t dev` and `databricks bundle deploy -t dev` to test an isolated, [dev <user>]-prefixed, schedule-paused copy.
2. They open a PR to main; GitHub Actions checks out the code, installs the CLI, and runs `databricks bundle validate -t staging` as a required status check.
3. A reviewer approves; on merge to main the deploy workflow authenticates to prod via the prod service principal and runs `databricks bundle deploy -t prod`.
4. The CLI builds the utilities wheel, syncs notebooks to the prod root path, and applies the job and DLT pipeline via Terraform-backed state, activating the production schedule.
5. A smoke step runs `databricks bundle run daily_sales_etl -t prod` and the DLT pipeline runs on its schedule; run status and failure emails route to the team.
endToEndExample.output: A production daily_sales_etl job and a DLT pipeline, both unprefixed with active schedules, running as a dedicated service principal, writing curated Delta tables into the main catalog, with the exact deployed config traceable to a Git commit.
endToEndExample.monitoring: Workflows run history and DLT pipeline event logs show execution status; system tables track job runs and costs; GitHub Actions logs record every validate/deploy with the commit SHA and target; failure emails alert on-call.
endToEndExample.errorHandling: validate on PR blocks broken config from merging; deploy is idempotent so a failed partial deploy is safely re-run from Terraform state; jobs define task retries and idempotent Delta writes so transient runtime failures self-heal; the prod GitHub Environment requires reviewer approval before deploy.
endToEndExample.finalResult: The team eliminated environment drift and accidental prod runs, gained code review on every infrastructure change, and can reproduce or roll back any deployment from Git, cutting release incidents and shortening the path from merge to production.

industryUseCases.problem: Dozens of nightly ETL jobs and dashboards were deployed manually, drifting between dev and prod and lacking review.
industryUseCases.solution: Model every job and DLT pipeline in Asset Bundles with dev/staging/prod targets and GitHub Actions running validate-on-PR and deploy-on-merge.
industryUseCases.benefits: Consistent, reviewable deployments; no environment drift; faster, safer releases with a full Git audit trail of what ran in prod.

industryUseCases.problem: Model training jobs, MLflow experiments, and serving endpoints needed reproducible, auditable promotion across regulated environments.
industryUseCases.solution: ML bundles package training jobs, experiments, and serving endpoints, deployed by service principals via CI/CD with per-target run-as identities and permissions as code.
industryUseCases.benefits: Auditable model promotion, least-privilege service-principal deploys, and reproducible environments satisfying compliance and change-management requirements.

industryUseCases.problem: Many product teams each reinvented deployment, producing inconsistent structure and no shared standards.
industryUseCases.solution: Publish custom bundle templates via `databricks bundle init` so every team scaffolds a standardized project with baked-in targets, naming, and CI/CD.
industryUseCases.benefits: Organization-wide consistency, faster onboarding, and centralized best practices that scale across dozens of repositories.

productionDeepDive.scalability: Split large configurations into multiple files pulled in via include, parameterize environment differences with variables, and standardize across many projects with bundle templates; a single CI/CD pipeline deploys many resources idempotently, and per-developer dev-mode deployments scale to large teams without collision.
productionDeepDive.faultTolerance: Terraform-backed state makes deploys idempotent, so a failed or interrupted deploy converges cleanly on re-run; runtime resilience is handled by defining task retries, timeouts, and idempotent Delta writes in the bundled jobs and pipelines.
productionDeepDive.highAvailability: Deployment is a control-plane operation; production jobs should use multi-AZ-capable clusters and DLT for automatic recovery, while the bundle ensures the correct, HA-friendly configuration is applied consistently on every deploy.
productionDeepDive.disasterRecovery: Because the entire project (code + infrastructure) is in Git, a workspace can be reconstructed by re-running `databricks bundle deploy -t prod` against a new or recovered workspace; Terraform state stored in the workspace should be considered when planning recovery, and critical variables/secrets backed up.
productionDeepDive.performanceOptimization: Keep bundles modular, cache and pin the CLI in CI to speed runs, define right-sized job clusters as code, and use artifacts to build wheels once and reuse them, minimizing both deploy time and runtime resource usage.
productionDeepDive.costOptimization: Dev mode pauses schedules and prefixes resources to prevent accidental prod-scale runs; define ephemeral job clusters (not always-on all-purpose clusters) in the bundle; destroy per-developer deployments after use; tag resources via the bundle for cost attribution.
productionDeepDive.securityConsiderations: Authenticate CI/CD with OAuth service principals or OIDC federation instead of long-lived PATs, scope one least-privilege service principal per environment, set run_as to a service principal in prod, gate the prod environment with required reviewers, and store secrets as per-environment CI secrets, never in the repo.
productionDeepDive.monitoringAndObservability: Track deployed jobs and pipelines through Workflows run history, DLT event logs, and system tables; correlate deployments with commits via CI logs; alert on deploy failures and on job/pipeline failures through email/webhook notifications defined in the bundle.
productionDeepDive.dataQualityValidation: Bundle DLT pipelines with expectations (@dlt.expect) so data quality rules deploy as code and enforce constraints on every run; add CI steps to run unit tests on the wheel before deploy to catch logic regressions early.
productionDeepDive.loggingAndAlerting: CI/CD logs capture every validate/deploy with target and commit SHA; configure email_notifications and webhook notifications in the bundled jobs; alert on deploy step failures in GitHub Actions and on anomalous service-principal activity for security.

recommendedPractices: **Keep code and infrastructure together** in one Git repo with the databricks.yml, and require PR review for every change.
**Run `databricks bundle validate` on every PR** as a required check before any deploy.
**Use targets with mode: development for dev** and mode: production for prod so isolation and safety are automatic.
**Authenticate CI/CD with OAuth service principals or OIDC**, one per environment, never long-lived personal access tokens.
engineeringStandards: All production jobs and pipelines must be defined in a bundle and deployed via CI/CD; no manual UI edits to bundle-managed resources.
Prod deploys must run as a dedicated service principal via run_as, and the prod environment must require reviewer approval.
Environment differences must be expressed via variables and per-target overrides, not by forking the configuration.
designRecommendations: Split resources into files under resources/ and compose them with include for readability and modularity.
Prefer ephemeral job clusters defined in the bundle over long-running all-purpose clusters.
Build shared library code as a wheel via the artifacts mapping instead of duplicating logic in notebooks.
namingConventions: Name bundles by data product or domain (e.g., sales_etl, ml_scoring).
Name targets by environment (dev, staging, prod) consistently across all bundles.
Rely on dev mode's [dev <username>] prefixing for isolation; keep prod resource names clean and unprefixed.
documentationStandards: Document each variable's purpose and default in the variables mapping description field.
Maintain a README describing how to validate, deploy, run, and destroy the bundle per target.
Document the service-principal identities and permissions used by each environment's CI/CD pipeline.
testingStrategies: Run unit tests on the packaged wheel in CI before `bundle deploy`.
Deploy to a dev target and smoke-run jobs before promoting to prod.
Add `databricks bundle validate -t <target>` for every target to a CI matrix to catch per-environment config errors.

commonMistakes.mistake: Editing bundle-managed jobs or pipelines directly in the Databricks UI.
commonMistakes.whyItHappens: It is faster to click in the UI than to change YAML and redeploy, especially for a quick fix.
commonMistakes.impact: The next `bundle deploy` overwrites the manual change because Terraform state converges to the declared config, causing confusing 'lost changes' and drift.
commonMistakes.correctApproach: Treat the bundle as the single source of truth: make changes in databricks.yml, review via PR, and redeploy; never hand-edit bundle-managed resources.

commonMistakes.mistake: Using long-lived personal access tokens for CI/CD authentication.
commonMistakes.whyItHappens: PATs are the quickest thing to paste into a secret and get a pipeline working.
commonMistakes.impact: Tokens expire (breaking pipelines) and represent a standing credential tied to a person, a security and continuity risk.
commonMistakes.correctApproach: Use OAuth machine-to-machine service principals (DATABRICKS_CLIENT_ID/SECRET) or OIDC federation, one least-privilege service principal per environment.

commonMistakes.mistake: Deploying to prod with mode: development (or no mode) and expecting production behavior.
commonMistakes.whyItHappens: Copy-pasting a dev target block or omitting mode leads to prefixed, schedule-paused resources in prod.
commonMistakes.impact: Production jobs never run on schedule (paused) or appear with [dev ...] prefixes, breaking downstream expectations.
commonMistakes.correctApproach: Explicitly set mode: production on the prod target so schedules stay active, names are clean, and validation is strict.

commonMistakes.mistake: Using the legacy Python CLI or dbx for bundle commands.
commonMistakes.whyItHappens: Older machines and docs reference the deprecated tooling.
commonMistakes.impact: bundle subcommands are unavailable or behave differently, and dbx is deprecated, wasting time and blocking CI.
commonMistakes.correctApproach: Install and pin the Go-based Databricks CLI (v0.200+), which natively supports bundle validate/deploy/run/destroy.

comparisonSection.explanation: DABs are a first-class, CLI-native, YAML-declarative IaC framework maintained by Databricks and GA. dbx was a separate, now-deprecated Python tool; new projects should use DABs, and existing dbx projects should migrate.

Bundles excel at application-level assets (jobs, DLT pipelines, schemas, ML) and hide Terraform behind a simple CLI. The raw Terraform provider is more expressive for account/workspace provisioning and complex networking but is heavier to author.

development prefixes resource names with [dev <user>], pauses schedules/triggers, and tags resources for safe, per-developer shared-workspace use. production deploys clean, unprefixed, schedule-active resources with stricter validation for real deployments.

OAuth service principals and OIDC provide non-personal, rotatable, least-privilege, environment-scoped credentials ideal for automation. PATs are person-tied, expire, and are a security/continuity risk, so they are discouraged for CI/CD.

beginnerQuestions.question: What is a Databricks Asset Bundle?
beginnerQuestions.answer: It is a declarative, YAML-defined project (rooted at databricks.yml) that packages source files and Databricks resources (jobs, DLT pipelines, schemas, experiments) together with deployment targets, deployed via the Databricks CLI as infrastructure-as-code.
beginnerQuestions.explanation: Emphasize that it unifies code and infrastructure and enables reproducible, Git-driven, environment-promoted deployments.

beginnerQuestions.question: What are the main sections of a databricks.yml file?
beginnerQuestions.answer: The top-level mappings are bundle (name/identity), include (extra files), variables (parameters), resources (jobs, pipelines, schemas, experiments), and targets (dev/staging/prod environments with overrides).
beginnerQuestions.explanation: Listing the sections shows you understand how a bundle is structured and composed.

intermediateQuestions.question: How do targets and mode: development vs production differ, and why does it matter?
intermediateQuestions.answer: Targets are named environments with their own workspace host and overrides. mode: development prefixes resource names with [dev <username>], pauses schedules and triggers, and tags resources for isolated, per-developer work in a shared workspace. mode: production deploys clean, unprefixed, schedule-active resources with stricter validation. It matters because it prevents accidental prod-scale runs from dev and avoids developer collisions.
intermediateQuestions.explanation: Highlight the safety behaviors mode drives and how targets enable promotion of the same code.

intermediateQuestions.question: How does variable substitution work in a bundle?
intermediateQuestions.answer: You declare variables under the variables mapping with defaults, then reference them as ${var.name}. Built-in substitutions like ${bundle.target}, ${bundle.name}, and ${workspace.current_user.userName} inject context. Values can be overridden per target or via CLI/env, and everything resolves at deploy time; validate fails if a required value is missing.
intermediateQuestions.explanation: Show that substitution keeps config DRY and environment-agnostic, resolved during validate/deploy.

advancedQuestions.question: How do Asset Bundles achieve idempotent, drift-free deployments internally?
advancedQuestions.answer: The CLI resolves the config (merging includes and target overrides, resolving variables), then generates a Terraform configuration and applies it, storing Terraform state in the workspace. Because state records what exists, each deploy computes and applies only the diff, converging the environment to the declared config. This makes deploys idempotent, corrects drift (including overwriting manual UI edits), and enables destroy to tear resources down cleanly.
advancedQuestions.explanation: A strong answer connects the developer-facing CLI to the Terraform state model and its consequences (idempotency, drift correction, destroy).

advancedQuestions.question: Design a secure CI/CD authentication scheme for deploying bundles to prod from GitHub Actions.
advancedQuestions.answer: Use OAuth machine-to-machine authentication with a dedicated service principal per environment, granting each only the permissions it needs. Store DATABRICKS_CLIENT_ID/SECRET as GitHub Environment secrets (or, better, use OIDC federation to avoid stored secrets entirely). Gate the prod GitHub Environment with required reviewers, set run_as to the service principal in the prod target, and run validate on PRs and deploy only on merge to main. Never use personal access tokens.
advancedQuestions.explanation: Look for least-privilege, per-environment, non-personal credentials, environment protection rules, and validate/deploy gating.

scenarioBasedQuestions.scenario: Your team of eight engineers shares one Databricks workspace and keeps clobbering each other's jobs and accidentally triggering scheduled prod-like runs while testing. How do you fix this with bundles?
scenarioBasedQuestions.thinkingProcess: The problem is isolation and accidental scheduled runs in a shared workspace. Dev mode solves both: prefixing prevents name collisions, and schedule pausing prevents accidental runs. Each developer deploys their own dev target copy.
scenarioBasedQuestions.expectedAnswer: Define a dev target with mode: development and default: true. Each engineer runs `databricks bundle deploy -t dev`, which prefixes their resources with [dev <username>], pauses all schedules/triggers, and tags resources, so deployments no longer collide and nothing runs on a schedule during testing. Prod stays a separate target with mode: production deployed only via CI/CD, so testing can never touch production.

systemDesignQuestions.problemStatement: Design an end-to-end CI/CD system for deploying dozens of Databricks jobs and DLT pipelines across dev, staging, and prod for multiple teams.
systemDesignQuestions.designApproach: Each data product is a bundle in its own repo, scaffolded from a shared bundle template (via bundle init) that bakes in standard targets, naming, and a GitHub Actions workflow. The workflow runs `databricks bundle validate -t staging` on PRs and `databricks bundle deploy -t prod` on merge to main, authenticating each environment with its own OAuth service principal via GitHub Environments. Resources are split under resources/ and composed with include; environment differences use variables and per-target overrides; shared code is built as wheels via artifacts.
systemDesignQuestions.tradeOffs: Bundles are lighter and more opinionated than raw Terraform but less expressive for account-level infrastructure, which is handled separately. Per-repo bundles maximize team autonomy but require a shared template to enforce standards. Ephemeral job clusters cut cost but add startup latency.
systemDesignQuestions.scalingStrategy: Standardize with templates so new projects onboard quickly; modularize configs with include; scale deploys with one least-privilege service principal per environment; use system tables and CI logs to observe deploys and runs across all teams.

cheatSheet.oneLineDefinition: Databricks Asset Bundles are the native YAML-based infrastructure-as-code framework (databricks.yml + Databricks CLI) for packaging and deploying jobs, pipelines, and ML assets across dev/staging/prod via CI/CD.
keyConcepts: databricks.yml sections: bundle, include, variables, resources, targets.
mode: development prefixes + pauses schedules; mode: production deploys clean, active resources.
Deploys are idempotent via Terraform state stored in the workspace.
CI/CD auth via OAuth service principals or OIDC, not PATs.
commands: databricks bundle validate -t <target>   # check resolved config
databricks bundle deploy -t <target>     # build, sync, apply resources
databricks bundle run <resource> -t <target>  # trigger a job/pipeline
databricks bundle summary -t <target>    # show deployed resource URLs
databricks bundle init                    # scaffold from a template
interviewPoints: DABs are the GA successor to dbx and require the Go-based CLI (v0.200+).
Targets + mode drive environment promotion and dev isolation.
Variables and substitution keep configuration DRY and environment-agnostic.
Terraform under the hood gives idempotent, drift-correcting deploys.
CI/CD: validate on PR, deploy on merge, authenticate with service principals/OIDC.
quickNotes: Never hand-edit bundle-managed resources in the UI; deploy overwrites drift.
Set default: true on the dev target so it is selected without -t.
Use run_as with a service principal in prod for consistent identity.
Split resources/*.yml and pull them in via include for readability.
Build shared code as a wheel via the artifacts mapping.
databricks/setup-cli installs the CLI in GitHub Actions runners.

keyTakeaways: Databricks Asset Bundles are the native infrastructure-as-code framework: a databricks.yml declares the bundle, included files, variables, resources (jobs, DLT pipelines, schemas, experiments), and targets, deployed by the Go-based Databricks CLI.

Targets and mode (development vs production) enable promoting the same code across environments while automatically prefixing/pausing dev resources and deploying clean, schedule-active prod resources.

Variable substitution (${var.x}, ${bundle.target}, ${workspace.current_user.userName}) plus per-target overrides keep configuration DRY, and deploys are idempotent because bundles use Terraform state under the hood.

CI/CD with GitHub Actions runs `databricks bundle validate` on PRs and `databricks bundle deploy` on merge, authenticating each environment with least-privilege OAuth service principals or OIDC rather than personal access tokens.

DABs replace dbx and manual UI/JSON deployment, providing a Git-driven, reviewable, auditable, drift-free deployment lifecycle for the entire Databricks project via validate, deploy, run, and destroy commands.
